title: Assessing functional adequacy in oral dialogic speech: Validating a rating scale for L2 interaction
text_snippet: Assessing functional adequacy in oral dialogic speech: Validating a rating scale for L2 interaction Functional Adequacy (FA), a multidimensional construct emphasising successful task completion, has developed into an established line of research in second language acquisition (SLA). Kuiken and Vedder’s (2017, 2018) FA rating scale, which operationalises FA across four dimensions (Task Requirements, Content, Comprehensibility, Coherence & Cohesion), has been shown to provide a reliable and valid instrument for assessing second language (L2) performance in monologic tasks. Contrary to monologue performance, few studies have, however, investigated L2 interaction due to its inherent complexity (Galaczi & Taylor, 2020). Recent research has called for adaptations of the FA monologue scale for dialogic data (González-Lloret, 2022). To this end, Kuiken and Vedder (2025) substituted the Coherence & Cohesion dimension of the monologue scale with a new dimension, Interaction, focusing on the adequacy of speakers’ engagement in situated communicative interaction. Our study explores the reliability, validity, and applicability of the adapted FA scale for interactional speech. title: Assessment of Task-Based Pragmatic Performance: Measuring Pragmatic Complexity and Accuracy
text_snippet: Assessment of Task-Based Pragmatic Performance: Measuring Pragmatic Complexity and Accuracy Assessing pragmatic performance is crucial in second language (L2) pedagogy, and it has recently gained attention within task-based research. Current studies commonly employ holistic or analytic rating scales to evaluate pragmatic performance, yet the reliability and interpretive consistency of such ratings remain debatable. This study proposes a refined approach by distinguishing between dimension-specific holistic ratings and quantitative index-based measures. It also introduces the concepts of pragmatic complexity and pragmatic accuracy to examine task-based pragmatic outcomes. Thirty-seven Czech L2 learners of English completed a simple and a complex decision-making task designed to elicit suggestion speech acts. In line with the Cognition Hypothesis, these tasks varied in cognitive complexity as reflected in the number of elements and reasoning demands. Raters used dimension-specific holistic rubrics to provide scores for pragmatic accuracy and complexity. Complementary indices—ratios of suggestion types and inaccuracies relative to total suggestions—yielded empirically derived indicators of pragmatic performance. title: The acquisition of generic reference by L1 Saudi Arabic learners of L2 English
text_snippet: The acquisition of generic reference by L1 Saudi Arabic learners of L2 English English and Arabic differ in their use of articles with genericity and this might affect learners’ accuracy. English has two types of genericity – the Noun Phrase (NP)-level generic (singular with the definite article and plural with bare plural nouns) and the sentence-level generic (singular with the indefinite article and plural with bare plural nouns) – while Arabic uses only the definite article, without differentiation. This study investigates the effects of first language (L1) transfer, proficiency level, receptive vocabulary and productive vocabulary on the acquisition of genericity. To examine generic contexts in English, 160 L1 Saudi Arabic learners of English completed an acceptability judgement task, receptive and productive vocabulary tasks and a proficiency test. The study outcomes, which relate to both low-level and high-level learners, show target-like performance for the use of the definite article with the NP singular but non-target-like performance with the NP plural and sentence singular and plural, in which the learners overused the definite article; these findings indicate the effect of L1 transfer.
